subject: Reading Comprehension
text: PASSAGE (SRC-01-P1): The cities of the Harappan civilisation are often admired for their grid-like streets, but their most revealing feature lies beneath those streets. Almost every house in towns such as Mohenjo-daro was connected to covered drains of baked brick that ran along the lanes and emptied into larger channels outside the settlement. Inspection holes were left at regular intervals, which suggests that the drains were cleaned and repaired rather than built once and forgotten. Such a system could not have been the work of individual households acting alone. It required agreement on the slope of streets, the size of bricks and the placement of each house, and it required someone to see that these rules were kept for generations. Historians therefore read the drains as evidence of a strong civic order, even though no palace, royal tomb or ruler's name has been found. Yet the absence of grand monuments also cautions against easy conclusions. The same order might have come from councils of merchants, from priests or from shared custom rather than from a single authority. What the drains prove beyond doubt is that the Harappans valued public health and long-term planning; who directed that planning remains an open question. || What is the central theme of the passage?
option_A: The history of town planning in the ancient world
option_B: Harappan drains reveal careful civic planning, though who directed it is still uncertain
option_C: The size of the bricks used in Harappan houses
option_D: Harappan cities were ruled by powerful kings who built their drains

subject: Reading Comprehension
text: PASSAGE (SRC-01-P2): For decades, the movement of young people from villages to cities has been described as a loss for the countryside. Fields are left to the elderly, schools lose pupils and festivals grow quieter. This picture is accurate as far as it goes, but it leaves out the money, ideas and contacts that travel back along the same roads. Remittances sent by migrant workers now pay for pucca houses, school fees and small shops in many villages, and returning workers often bring skills in construction, tailoring or repair that were not available locally before. Mobile phones have also made it possible for families to stay closely involved in one another's decisions despite living hundreds of kilometres apart. None of this means that migration is costless. Households whose only earner is away for most of the year carry heavy burdens, and villages that depend on remittances are exposed when urban jobs disappear, as many discovered during sudden economic shocks. The more useful question, then, is not whether migration helps or harms the village, but how the village can turn the flows it already receives into lasting local opportunity. || Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
option_C: Migration and the Village: Loss and Return
option_D: Why Villages Gain Nothing from Migration
